strengths: The paper addresses a clear and well-motivated gap: existing latent space models for NCO either require labeled data (CVAE-Opt) or instance-independent latent spaces (COMPASS). LGS-Net's instance-conditioned latent space is a sensible and well-positioned contribution, clearly differentiated from prior work in Section 2.

The theoretical analysis is substantive: Proposition 5.1 and Theorem 5.1 establish reversibility and geometric ergodicity (in TV and L2) of the fixed-θ chain via a careful minorization/drift argument (Appendix C), and Section 5.2/Appendix D provides convergence results for the time-inhomogeneous chain with SA updates, a setting the authors correctly note is not covered by existing adaptive MCMC theory (Andrieu & Atchadé 2007; Douc et al. 2004). The error decomposition into mixing, tracking, and optimization terms in Theorem 5.2 is informative and well-interpreted.

The empirical evaluation is thorough and convincing within its scope: standard TSP/CVRP benchmarks with 100/125/150 nodes, comparisons against POMO, CVAE-Opt, EAS, COMPASS, LKH3, and Concorde, both with and without the augmentation trick, plus useful ablations (Table 3, Figure 3) isolating the contribution of interacting MCMC and the SA update. The gains over COMPASS without augmentation are notable, and the negative-gap results on CVRP n=100/125 are strong evidence.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: source code is publicly available, and Appendix E gives detailed architecture, training, proposal distribution, and update-schedule specifications.
The ablation study in Table 3 thoughtfully distinguishes LGS from parallel MCMC, single MCMC, DE, CMA-ES, and EAS, directly supporting the claim that joint sampling and parameter updating matters.
weaknesses: There is a potential soundness gap in the theory-to-practice link for K > 1. The interacting proposal in Appendix E.2 has q(z^k | z^{1:K}) depend on another particle's previous state (z^l with random l), meaning the K chains are not independent. Yet the extension in Appendix C.3 analyzes the kernel as a product of K independent copies, and Theorem 5.1's extension to K > 1 is argued via component-wise reversibility. The manuscript does not reconcile the interacting proposal actually used at inference with the product-kernel analysis, leaving the applicability of Theorem 5.1 to the practical algorithm unclear.

Theorem 5.2 conditions on Assumption 4, i.e., that θ_m converges to some θ_∞ at a rate a_m — this effectively assumes the conclusion that the SA converges. Appendix D.3 argues this 'can be satisfied' under additional smoothness assumptions by analogy with prior biased-SA analyses, but this is a sketch rather than a proof, so the headline claim of 'rigorous convergence guarantees' for the full algorithm (with SA) is weaker than advertised.

The theoretical contribution, while carefully executed, is largely an assembly of standard tools (Meyn–Tweedie drift/minorization, coupling arguments from Douc et al. 2018) applied to a Metropolis–Hastings chain on a product space; the genuinely new technical content (time-inhomogeneous case with evolving target) is the part that relies on the circular assumption above.

The state-of-the-art claim needs qualification: EAS outperforms LGS on CVRP n=150 with augmentation, and LGS requires substantially more inference compute than POMO (e.g., 20M–80M vs. <1M), which is only partially discussed.

Evaluation is limited to two routing problems with n ≤ 150 on uniform distributions; scalability of the latent-space approach (both memory of the K particles and the small fixed latent dimension) to larger or structured instances is unaddressed, and the problem-setting framing suggests broader applicability (Knapsack, Job Scheduling) that is never tested.

Key hyperparameters (K, the SA update schedule {1, 5, 15, 25, 100, 150}, proposal variance and scaling γ) are chosen manually 'without extensive hyperparameter tuning'; the authors themselves flag schedule selection as open, which limits confidence that reported numbers are robust.
There is no dedicated limitations discussion in the main paper; limitations are scattered or only implied (e.g., compute cost, manual schedules, EAS's advantage at n=150).

strengths: The paper provides genuinely rigorous theoretical analysis: geometric ergodicity of the Metropolis-Hastings kernel for fixed parameters (Theorem 5.1), and a new convergence result for time-inhomogeneous MCMC with Stochastic Approximation (Theorem 5.2) that avoids restrictive convexity/coercivity assumptions. The proofs in Appendices C and D are detailed and largely self-contained.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: both TSP and CVRP, with and without the augmentation trick, out-of-distribution generalization (n=125, 150), comparisons against multiple strong baselines (POMO, EAS, COMPASS, CVAE-Opt) and exact/heuristic solvers (Concorde, LKH3, OR-Tools), plus ablations on the inference method (Table 3) and hyperparameter studies (Figures 6, 7).

The ablation cleanly separates the contribution of interacting MCMC and the SA parameter update from simpler baselines (single MCMC, parallel MCMC, DE, CMA-ES), supporting the claim that joint sampling and parameter updating is what drives the gains.
Source code is publicly available, and training/inference details (architecture, optimizer, proposal distribution, update schedules) are documented in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to prior latent-space NCO work. The model is a close variant of CVAE-Opt (Hottung et al., 2021) and COMPASS (Chalumeau et al., 2023) - essentially an instance-conditioned latent space plus REINFORCE-style training with an entropy/weighting scheme from Grinsztajn et al. (2023). The main new element is the MCMC+SA inference scheme, so the contribution rests heavily on that inference algorithm.

The practical significance of the convergence theory is questionable. Theorem 5.2 only guarantees convergence of the chain to the stationary distribution pi_{theta_infty} of the *current* parameters, and Assumption 4 merely requires theta_infty to be a critical point. Convergence to a possibly suboptimal stationary distribution says little about solution quality - the gap between the theoretical guarantee and the reported optimality gaps is not bridged.

Several theoretical assumptions are quite strong and arguably artificial: bounded cost, positivity of the encoder/decoder distributions everywhere on the latent space, and an implicitly compact latent region (drift analysis uses a ball of radius R; in practice the latent space is a ball of radius 40). The epsilon constants in the minorization condition are likely astronomically small, so the geometric rates (rho, kappa) have no practical quantitative meaning.

The evaluation is confined to two routing problems at small scale (n <= 150). Despite framing the model for general CO (the problem setting explicitly covers Knapsack, Job Scheduling, etc.), no non-routing or larger-scale experiments are provided, weakening the generality claims made in the introduction.

Fairness of the computational budget comparisons is unclear: reported inference times range from <1M to 20M-80M operations across methods, and the paper acknowledges that reducing the number of latent samples hurts CVRP n=150 performance, where EAS then wins. It is hard to tell whether the reported SOTA reflects a genuinely better method or simply more inference compute in most settings.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is substantial and handled ad hoc: the SA update interval schedule [1, 5, 15, 25, 100, 150] is chosen manually without tuning, the authors concede that choosing these intervals is 'non-trivial' and leave schedule optimization as an open problem, and Figure 6 shows gains from increasing K plateau quickly with high variance across runs.

Presentation issues: the paper is dense, key experimental details (SA performed only at selected intervals, contradicting the analysis setup in Algorithm 1 which updates theta every iteration) are deferred to the experiments section, creating a mismatch between the theory analyzed and the algorithm actually evaluated.

No discussion of limitations is included, and the conclusion overstates the contribution ('setting a new benchmark') without acknowledging the narrow problem scope and the assumptions underlying the theory.

strengths: The paper combines a practical inference algorithm with genuinely relevant theory: Theorem 5.1 establishes geometric ergodicity of the fixed-θ chain (TV and L2), and Theorem 5.2 extends this to the time-inhomogeneous setting induced by stochastic approximation updates — a setting the authors correctly note is not covered by existing adaptive MCMC results (Andrieu & Atchadé 2007; Douc et al. 2004) because both kernel and target evolve. The proofs (Appendices C–D) verify minorization and Foster–Lyapunov drift conditions carefully and do not rely on unrealistic convexity/coercivity assumptions; Assumption 4 (convergence to a critical point rather than a unique minimizer) is appropriately weak for a non-convex inference objective.

The experimental evaluation is convincing for the scope claimed: TSP and CVRP at n = 100/125/150, with and without the augmentation trick, against strong baselines (POMO, CVAE-Opt, EAS, COMPASS) plus exact/industrial solvers (Concorde, LKH-3, OR-Tools). The method achieves near-optimal TSP gaps without augmentation and consistently outperforms baselines on OOD instances, and beats LKH-3 on CVRP at n = 100/125. The claims are properly scoped to 'state-of-the-art among RL-based methods'.

The ablations are informative and well-designed: Table 3 and Figure 3 disentangle the contributions of parallel MCMC, interacting MCMC, and the SA update, demonstrating that parameter updating during inference (not just better mixing) is the key driver — this directly connects the empirical gains to the theoretical analysis. Figure 2 gives an intuitive visualization of the learned latent landscape and search trajectory.

Reproducibility is good: source code is publicly available, and Appendices A and E provide full architectural, training, and inference details (hyperparameters, proposal distribution, update schedule, batch sizes, hardware), enabling faithful reimplementation.

The positioning relative to prior latent-space approaches (CVAE-Opt requiring labeled data; COMPASS requiring a pretrained policy and instance-independent latents) is clear and accurate, and the instance-conditioned latent model genuinely addresses a real limitation of prior work without needing the augmentation trick.
weaknesses: The contribution is somewhat incremental in the model component: LGS-Net is essentially a CVAE-style latent model with an instance-conditioned encoder, i.e., a relatively natural combination of CVAE-Opt (Hottung et al. 2021) and COMPASS (Chalumeau et al. 2023) ideas, trained with a max-entropy RL loss similar to Grinsztajn et al. (2023). The main novelty lies in the inference scheme (LGS) and its analysis rather than the model itself.

The practical relevance of the theory has limits: convergence is to the reweighted distribution π_θ of Eq. (3), not to optimal solutions, and the constants (ρ, κ) arising from the minorization condition are not computed, so the theorems guarantee qualitative convergence but give no usable quantitative guidance. Moreover, in the experiments the SA updates are performed only at selected intervals rather than every iteration (Section 6, App. E.2), which deviates from the analyzed Algorithm 1; while arguably still within the time-inhomogeneous framework, this gap between theory and practice is not formally addressed.

The theoretical assumptions, while standard, are somewhat strong in practice: strict positivity of the decoder probabilities for all feasible nodes (softmax with masking implies exactly zero probability for infeasible nodes, contradicting Assumption 1 as literally stated for masked entries) and positivity of the encoder density on all of Z deserve more careful discussion.

Scope of empirical validation is narrow: only two Euclidean routing problems with up to 150 nodes, both with coordinates in the unit square. The claimed advantage of avoiding the augmentation trick is only tested on problems where augmentation applies anyway; broader problem classes (Knapsack, scheduling, non-Euclidean variants mentioned in Section 3.2) are untested. The reduction in K at n = 150 for CVRP with augmentation, causing the method to fall behind EAS, suggests sensitivity to the computational budget that is only partially explored.

Main result tables report single objective/gap values without variance or confidence intervals across inference runs (Figure 3 shows mean over 10 runs, but Table 1/2 do not clarify averaging), and some key hyperparameters (SA update schedule, γ, β) were 'chosen manually without extensive hyperparameter tuning', which weakens the strength of the comparison against heavily tuned baselines like EAS and COMPASS.

Minor presentation issues: a few typos and inconsistent statements (e.g., 'Computation of Log-Probabilities' header repeated for softmax outputs; Figure 6 x-axis labeled ε but discussed as K; the λ in Eq. (3) vs. the reweighting description in Section 4.3/6 is slightly confusing).

strengths: The paper combines a new instance-conditioned latent space model (LGS-Net) with a novel inference scheme (LGS) that interleaves interacting MCMC over latents with stochastic-approximation updates of decoder parameters — a well-motivated combination that addresses real limitations of prior latent-space NCO methods (CVAE-Opt's reliance on labeled data; COMPASS's instance-independent prior).

The theoretical contribution is non-trivial: geometric ergodicity for the fixed-θ kernel via minorization/drift conditions on the joint (z,y) space, and new convergence results for time-inhomogeneous MCMC with SA updates (Theorem D.1), where the error decomposition into mixing, tracking, and optimization error is clean and the proofs appear careful and largely self-contained.

The empirical evaluation is extensive and convincing: SOTA among NCO baselines on TSP/CVRP (n=100–200) with and without the augmentation trick, comparisons against exact/heuristic solvers (Concorde, LKH3, HGS, OR-Tools), and a rich set of ablations (inference method comparisons in Table 2/Fig. 2, loss comparison vs POPPY, instance-conditioned vs instance-independent and stochastic vs deterministic latent models, diffusion prior, latent dimension/radius, SA update frequency, knapsack extension).

Reproducibility is well handled: source code is public, hyperparameters, hardware, and the wall-clock budget methodology are documented, and the fairness of budget allocation across baselines is explicitly justified.
The limitations discussion (scaling to large instances, constraints not expressible via decoder masking, manual choice of update schedules) is honest and substantive rather than superficial.
weaknesses: There is a gap between the theory and the algorithm actually run: the adaptive-θ analysis (Theorem 5.3 / Algorithm 4) covers only K=1 without interaction, whereas experiments use K=600 interacting particles; the fixed-θ result covers general K but not the SA component. Convergence guarantees for the full algorithm as implemented are therefore not established.

Assumption 4 (||θm − θ∞|| = O(am)) essentially assumes the SA iterates converge to a limit; Appendix D.3 only argues heuristically that it 'can be satisfied' under additional smoothness assumptions. This weakens the force of Theorem 5.3, which also guarantees convergence only to π_θ∞ (a distribution depending on wherever θ happens to settle), not to any distribution favoring good solutions — the practical relevance of the guarantees to optimization quality is limited.

The novelty is somewhat incremental: each ingredient (latent-space NCO, MH sampling over latents, test-time parameter fine-tuning as in EAS/Active Search, entropy-regularized RL training) exists in prior work; the contribution is their composition plus instance conditioning. The paper positions this well, but the conceptual delta over COMPASS/CVAE-Opt is moderate.

Evaluation is confined to routing problems plus one small knapsack experiment; 'generalization' is tested only on larger instance sizes (n=125/150/200) from the same uniform distribution, not genuine distribution shift (e.g., clustered, non-uniform, or real-world instances), so claims about robust OOD behavior are only partially supported.

Several details require trust rather than verification: the claim that the bias of the inference gradient estimator is O(1/K), the justification for the manually chosen SA schedule [1,1,5,15,25,100,150], and the statement that solutions 'visually appear to be optimal' are under-supported relative to the rigor elsewhere.

strengths: The paper addresses a real limitation of prior latent-space NCO methods (CVAE-Opt requires labeled data; COMPASS uses an instance-independent latent prior) by proposing an instance-conditioned latent model trained with RL, which is a clear and well-motivated contribution.

The inference scheme (LGS) combining interacting MCMC over a continuous latent space with Stochastic Approximation updates of decoder parameters at test time is a novel inference mechanism, and the paper provides a formal treatment: Markov property, reversibility, geometric ergodicity (Thm 5.2), and a time-inhomogeneous convergence result (Thm 5.3) with an error decomposition into mixing, tracking, and optimization terms.

The empirical evaluation is broad and fairly careful: TSP/CVRP at n=100/125/150 (plus n=200 and knapsack in the appendix), comparisons against strong baselines (POMO, EAS, COMPASS, ELG, CNF, LKH3, Concorde, OR-Tools), results both with and without the augmentation trick, and a fixed wall-clock budget protocol.

The ablations are genuinely informative and isolate the claimed design choices: stochastic vs. deterministic latents (Table 8), instance-conditioned vs. instance-independent prior (Table 7), cost-weighted loss vs. POPPY (Table 6), inference-method comparison (Table 2), and hyperparameter sensitivity (Figures 6-8, Table 12). Code is stated to be publicly available, and implementation details are given.

The paper is honest about limitations: scaling to large instances, constraints not expressible via decoder masking, and the difficulty of choosing the SA update schedule are discussed openly rather than hidden.
weaknesses: There is a significant gap between the theory and the algorithm actually run. The fixed-θ analysis (Prop. C.1, Thm 5.2) is proven for K=1 with a per-particle proposal; the K>1 extension in C.3 treats the chains as independent products, but the practical proposal in the experiments is cross-particle (q depends on the whole population z_{1:K}), which is not the kernel analyzed. Similarly, inference is batched over 1,000 instances, which the per-instance theory does not cover.

The theoretical guarantees are likely vacuous in practice. The minorization constant ε involves ε_d = inf over the compact latent space of decoder probabilities and ε_q = inf of the proposal density in dimension d_z = 100; these quantities are astronomically small, so the 'geometric' rates κρ^m carry no practical information. The convergence result (Thm 5.3) additionally requires Assumption 4 (θ_m → θ_∞), which is assumed rather than established; Appendix D.3 only offers a heuristic argument that the assumption 'can be satisfied' under extra smoothness conditions that are not verified.

The headline empirical claims deserve scrutiny. Negative gaps vs. LKH3 on CVRP (e.g., -0.102%) suggest the LKH3 configuration used as reference may be under-tuned; several baselines (ELG, CNF) perform substantially worse than in their original papers under the chosen budget; and with the augmentation trick at n=150, EAS outperforms the proposed method. The wall-clock-budget protocol (budgets derived from the authors' own implementation, all methods run in the authors' PyTorch codebase on one GPU) may favor the proposed method, and 'state-of-the-art among NCO baselines' rests partly on this choice.

The practical contribution over the closest competitor (COMPASS + a strong continuous search) is not fully disentangled. The COMPASS + LGS experiment (Table 7) underperforms, but the explanation given (COMPASS's latent space usage) is speculative; the relative contributions of the reweighting factor, interaction, and SA updates are shown (Figure 2) but the aggregate margin over COMPASS/EAS is often within a few hundredths of a percent of gap, with no statistical significance testing reported.

Scope is narrow despite the general framing: the theory assumes compact latent space and finite solution space, and the experiments are essentially routing problems plus a small knapsack illustration; constrained problems requiring more than masking are explicitly left open, limiting the significance of the 'general framework' narrative.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated and clearly positioned relative to prior latent-space NCO methods (CVAE-Opt, COMPASS): the instance-conditioned latent prior is a natural and sensible fix to a real limitation of prior work, and the paper explains the design choices.

The theoretical section is unusually substantive for an NCO paper: geometric ergodicity for fixed θ (Theorem 5.2) and convergence of the time-inhomogeneous chain with SA updates (Theorem 5.3) are non-trivial results, with full proofs in the appendix adapting coupling arguments (Douc et al.) to a setting where both kernel and target evolve.

The empirical evaluation is comprehensive and fair: comparisons under matched wall-clock budgets, both with and without the augmentation trick, multiple problems (TSP, CVRP, knapsack, n up to 200), and extensive ablations (K, latent dimension, radius R, SA update schedule, deterministic vs. stochastic latents, instance-conditioned vs. independent, POPPY vs. cost-weighted loss, diffusion prior). The ablation in Table 2/8 that decomposes gains into particle propagation, interaction, and SA is particularly convincing.

Reproducibility is good: code is stated to be public, hyperparameters and hardware are documented, and the inference-budget selection procedure is explained. The limitations section (scaling, constraints not expressible via masking) is honest and thoughtful rather than defensive.
The empirical results genuinely advance the state of the art among learning-based NCO baselines on the standard benchmark suite, including beating LKH3 on some CVRP settings.
weaknesses: There is a meaningful gap between the theory and the algorithm as evaluated. The theory covers K=1 chains (then a product-kernel extension), per-instance updates, and assumes θm converges to some θ∞ (Assumption 4/8), which largely assumes the conclusion of the SA analysis; the justification in Appendix D.3 defers to additional smoothness and bias/variance conditions that are not verified for the actual estimator. In practice the method uses K=600 particles, a cross-particle proposal, Adam-like updates at irregular scheduled intervals, and — importantly — is run on batches of ~100 instances, raising the question of whether θ updates are shared across instances, which would deviate from the per-instance analysis.

The extension to K>1 (Appendix C.3) appears to ignore the interaction in the proposal: the cross-particle proposal q(z|z; z_m^{1:K}) makes the joint kernel over particles non-product, yet the proof writes a product kernel with per-particle proposals. The symmetry argument in F.2.1 is conditional on the population and suggests a fixed-θ detailed balance may still hold, but this is not rigorously connected to the K>1 ergodicity proof.

The constants underlying the convergence rates are likely vacuous in practice: uniform minorization requires an infimum of decoder probabilities over all z and feasible y (ε_d), which for softmax decoders and n=100–200 can be astronomically small, so Theorem 5.2/5.3 are best read as qualitative guarantees rather than predictive rates. The paper does not discuss the magnitudes of these constants.

Statistical rigor of the headline comparisons is thin: main tables appear to be single runs; only Figure 2 reports means over 10 runs. Many gaps that underpin the SOTA claim are small (e.g., 0.002% vs. 0.014% vs. COMPASS; -0.102% vs. -0.057% with augmentation), and no significance tests or confidence intervals are provided.

The negative-gap result versus LKH3 on CVRP is valid given LKH3 is heuristic, but the paper should be more careful in the abstract/introduction, where 'outperforms' claims could be misread as dominating exact/reference solutions; HGS results relegated to a table show a clear gap to the true state of the art in classical solvers, which is fine but should be framed consistently.

Scope is limited to medium instances (n ≤ 200) and constructive-maskable constraints; the paper acknowledges this, but the practical significance beyond the standard benchmark regime remains unproven, and the SA update schedule is manually hand-tuned ([1,1,5,15,25,100,150]), which weakens the plug-and-play claim of the inference method.
